communities.report: This community links two distinct clusters—art museum leadership and American secondary education geography—through shared entities of place and organization. At its center is Brian Kennedy (gallery director), full name Brian Patrick Kennedy, born 5 November 1961, an Irish-born art museum director who was born in and has worked in Ireland, has also worked in Australia, and now lives and works in the United States; his career trajectory includes serving as director of the National Gallery of Australia (located in Canberra) from 1997 to 2004, director of the Hood Museum of Art from 2005 to 2010, director of the Toledo Museum of Art (located in Ohio) from 2010 to 2019, and currently serving as director of the Peabody Essex Museum. A separate but connected figure, Ian Barry, is an Australian director of film and TV, tied to Australia as his country of nationality, the same country where Kennedy worked. The second cluster concerns East High School (Denver), a public high school located in the City Park neighborhood on the east side of Denver, Colorado, United States, which is part of the Denver Public Schools system; East High School is one of the four original high schools in Denver, alongside North High School, South High School, and West High School. Colorado is located in the United States, and Denver is located in Colorado. The final cluster centers on North Marion High School (Oregon), a public high school located in Aurora, Oregon, United States, which is part of the North Marion School District (a district that includes North Marion High School and three other schools, all on the same campus); Aurora, Oregon is located in the United States and draws students to this school, along with the communities of Broadacres, Butteville, Donald, and Hubbard, all of which draw students from North Marion High School. communities.report: This community centers on the House of Ascania, the German noble dynasty that ruled the principality of Anhalt-Zerbst across several generations. The genealogical chain begins with Albert I, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, whose second wife was Agnes, daughter of Conrad, Margrave of Brandenburg-Stendal; Agnes was the eldest child born to Albert I from this marriage and bore him two sons, Waldemar I, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (died 7 January 1368) and Albert II, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (died 17 July 1362), both rulers of Anhalt-Zerbst and members of the House of Ascania. Albert II married Beatrix, daughter of Rudolf I, Elector of Saxony and Duke of Saxe-Wittemberg, as his second wife; with her he had his eldest son Albert III, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (died ca. 1 August 1359), also a ruler of Anhalt-Zerbst and House of Ascania member, and his youngest son John II, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (died 11 April 1382), likewise a ruler of Anhalt-Zerbst and House of Ascania member. John II married Elisabeth, daughter of John I, Count of Henneberg-Schleusingen, and their youngest son was Waldemar III, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (died 1391), who also ruled Anhalt-Zerbst as a House of Ascania member. A separate but related line traces through John V, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, who married Margaret, daughter of Joachim I Nestor, Elector of Brandenburg; John V was the father of both Bernhard VII, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (born 17 March 1540, died 1 March 1570, both in Dessau) and, as his eldest son, Karl I, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (born 17 November 1534 in Dessau, died 4 May 1561 in Zerbst). Both Bernhard VII and Karl I were rulers of Anhalt-Zerbst and members of the House of Ascania, and both were sons of Margaret. Another branch runs through Rudolph, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, whose second wife was Magdalene, daughter of John VII, Count of Oldenburg; their son was John VI, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst (born in Zerbst on 24 March 1621, died in Zerbst on 4 July 1667), who ruled Anhalt-Zerbst and belonged to the House of Ascania. Throughout, Anhalt-Zerbst is repeatedly identified as the principality governed successively by Waldemar I, Albert II, Albert III, John II, Waldemar III, Bernhard VII, Karl I, and John VI, all bound together by House of Ascania membership and interlinked marriages to daughters of prominent noble houses including Brandenburg-Stendal, Saxe-Wittemberg, Henneberg-Schleusingen, Brandenburg (Joachim I Nestor's line), and Oldenburg.

members: The Return of Dr. Fu Manchu
communities.report: This community centers on the fictional villain Fu Manchu, created by author Sax Rohmer, and traces his cinematic history across multiple films spanning different eras and actors. The character first appeared in the talkie era with "The Mysterious Dr. Fu Manchu" (1929), an American pre-Code drama film directed by Rowland V. Lee and starring Warner Oland as the title character; in this film, Fu Manchu appeared to die, seeking revenge for the deaths of his wife and child. Rowland V. Lee also directed the 1930 sequel, "The Return of Dr. Fu Manchu," an American pre-Code film that continued as the second of three films starring Warner Oland as Fu Manchu. The most notable installment, "The Mask of Fu Manchu" (1932), is a pre-Code adventure film directed by Charles Brabin and based on Sax Rohmer's 1932 novel of the same name; its screenplay was co-written by Edgar Allan Woolf, Irene Kuhn, and John Willard. This film starred Boris Karloff in the role of Fu Manchu, with the central plot involving the villain's quest for the golden sword and mask of the historical Genghis Khan. The cast also featured Lewis Stone as Fu Manchu's nemesis and Myrna Loy as his depraved daughter; notably, the character Dr. Petrie does not appear in this film. The Fu Manchu film series continued through five installments, culminating in "The Castle of Fu Manchu" (1969), also known as "The Torture Chamber of Dr. Fu Manchu" and "Die Folterkammer des Dr. Fu Man Chu," which served as the fifth and final film in the series and starred Christopher Lee, who portrayed the title character Dr. Fu Manchu. Beyond the official series, "The Mask of Fu Manchu" also influenced later cinema, inspiring the 1984 erotic thriller "Les Trottoirs de Bangkok" (also known as "Bangkok Interdit"), which was directed by Jean Rollin.

This community centers on two distinct film-history threads connected through preservation institutions and directorial careers. The first thread concerns "Luck in Pawn," a 1919 American silent romance film directed by Walter Edwards and starring Marguerite Clark, based on a play written by Marvin Taylor; the play itself had a brief run on Broadway in 1919. The film was produced by Famous Players-Lasky and distributed through Paramount Pictures, and it survives today in preserved form at both the Library of Congress and the New Zealand Film Archive. The Library of Congress, in turn, is the institution responsible for maintaining the United States National Film Registry, the official registry of films selected for preservation. The second thread focuses on John Eliot Sturges (January 3, 1910 – August 18, 1992), an American film director explicitly noted as not related to fellow director Preston Sturges, despite the shared surname. John Sturges directed a substantial body of work, including "The Girl in White" (1952), a film drama based on the memoirs of pioneering female surgeon Emily Dunning Barringer; "Bad Day at Black Rock" (1955); "Gunfight at the O.K. Corral" (1957); "The Magnificent Seven" (1960); "The Great Escape" (1963); and "Ice Station Zebra" (1968). Among these, "The Magnificent Seven" holds particular historical distinction, having been selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry in 2013, thereby linking Sturges's directorial legacy back to the same Library of Congress-administered preservation system that safeguards "Luck in Pawn."

members: The Strange World of Planet X
communities.report: This community centers on director Bill Rebane and his body of low-budget science fiction and horror films, alongside a network of related filmmakers, actors, and institutions. Bill Rebane directed several notable works, including Invasion from Inner Earth (a 1974 apocalyptic science fiction film also known as Hell Fire and They), Monster A Go-Go (1965), Monster A-Go-Go, The Giant Spider Invasion (1975), and The Capture of Bigfoot (1979, also known as The Legend of Bigfoot). Invasion from Inner Earth starred actors Debbi Pick and Paul Bentzen, was filmed in the style of thrillers directed by Alfred Hitchcock, and was inspired by the 1957 British film The Strange World of Planet X. Monster a Go-Go, a 1965 American science-fiction horror film widely considered one of the worst films ever made, was directed by Bill Rebane but also directed, uncredited, by Herschell Gordon Lewis, an American filmmaker (June 15, 1926 – September 26, 2016) known for pioneering the "splatter" subgenre of horror. All Movie, a publication, reviewed Herschell Gordon Lewis' career, describing him as a pioneer in gore films, and he is linked to filmmaker Lucio Fulci, as both are called the "Godfather of Gore." Monster a Go-Go gained further notoriety when it was featured in a 1993 episode of Mystery Science Theater 3000, a satirical film-riffing television series that aired on the Comedy Central television network. Separately, The Capture of Bigfoot was originally produced and released by Studio Film Corp, and was later re-released in 2010 by Troma Entertainment.

This community centers on Marie Zéphyrine of France, a French princess born 26 August 1750 and died 2 September 1755 at the Palace of Versailles, which was both her birthplace and place of death; she was known during her short life as "Madame Royale" or "la Petite Madame." She was named after St Zephyrinus, whose feast day coincided with her birth. She was the daughter of Louis, Dauphin of France (born 4 September 1729, died 20 December 1765), the elder and only surviving son of King Louis XV, and his wife Maria Josepha of Saxony, who suffered stillbirths and had fragile health. Louis, Dauphin of France, though never himself becoming king, was a pivotal dynastic figure: he was the son of Louis XV and Queen Marie Leszczyńska, had a younger brother named Philippe who died as a toddler, and fathered three future kings of France—Louis XVI (reigned 1774–1792), Louis XVIII (reigned 1814–1815 and 1815–1824), and Charles X (reigned 1824–1830)—making him father to Marie Zéphyrine of France as well as to these three monarchs. At the time of Marie Zéphyrine's birth, her grandfather Louis XV had hoped for a grandson instead. Her governess was Marie Isabelle de Rohan, who served in that role for the young princess. In the days before her death, Marie Zéphyrine was baptised by the Abbot of Chabannes. Upon her death at Versailles in 1755, she was buried at the Royal Basilica of Saint Denis, a site located outside Paris. Tangential to this royal lineage, the community also includes Claude Weisz, a French film director born in Paris, connected to the network only through the shared location of Paris.

This community centers on the 1980 Christmas animated television special "A Snow White Christmas," which was produced by the animation studio Filmation and telecast on December 19, 1980, on the CBS television network. "A Snow White Christmas" serves as a sequel to the fairy tale "Snow White," and its plot centers on the Wicked Queen, the villain from "Snow White," who returns to life during Christmas and casts an evil spell, acting as the central antagonist whose return drives the plot. Within the special's narrative, Snow White's young daughter (referred to as Snow White (daughter)) escapes the Queen's spell and takes refuge with a dwarf friend and with the seven giants; the Wicked Queen must defeat these seven giants in order to save the kingdom. Filmation also produced another film, "Happily Ever After" (1990), which is likewise a sequel to "Snow White" but is explicitly unrelated to "A Snow White Christmas," despite both being produced by the same studio. Separately, the community includes Alice Washburn (1860–1929), an American stage and film actress who died of a heart attack in November 1929. Washburn worked at several early film studios—Edison, Vitagraph, and Kalem—and starred in "Snow White," which was her final film and her only known feature film.

This community centers on English model and actress Liberty Ross, born 23 September 1978, whose modeling and acting career included appearances in Vogue, Harper's Bazaar, and Dazed & Confused. She is the sister of composers Atticus Ross and Leopold Ross. Liberty Ross played the role of Queen Eleanor in the 2012 fantasy film Snow White and the Huntsman, which was directed by Rupert Sanders, her then-husband. The film also connects to Pakistani fashion and costume designer Maheen Khan, an award-winning designer who undertook embroidery work for Snow White and the Huntsman. Maheen Khan also undertook embroidery for the television series The Jewel in the Crown. In addition to her costume and embroidery work, Maheen Khan designs for two fashion labels she founded: The Embroidery HouseMaheen and Gulabo.

This community centers on John, Count Palatine of Neumarkt (Johann von Pfalz-Neumarkt, 1383 – 14 March 1443), who held the county palatine of Neumarkt from 1410 until his death in 1443, and was the son of Rupert III of the Palatinate. In 1407, John married Catherine of Pomerania (c. 1390 – 4 March 1426), a Pomeranian princess who became Countess Palatine of Neumarkt through this union. Catherine was the mother of Christopher of Bavaria, who rose to become king of the Kalmar Union, ruling simultaneously over the kingdoms of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway. On the military front, John achieved a significant and crushing victory in 1433 at the Battle of Hiltersried, decisively defeating the Hussites, a prominent religious and military movement of the era.

members: Wearing Velvet Slippers under a Golden Umbrella
communities.report: This community centers on the 1970 Burmese film Wearing Velvet Slippers under a Golden Umbrella (pronounced Katipa phanat see shwe htee hsaung), which was based on a novel of the same name written by novelist Maung Thara. The film marked the feature directorial debut of Maung Wunna, a two-time Myanmar Motion Picture Academy Awards-winning Burmese director and writer, who also wrote the film's screenplay; Maung Wunna later died of lung cancer in 2011. The film starred actors Myat Lay, Myat Mon, and Thet Naung. Maung Wunna came from a family deeply embedded in Myanmar's entertainment industry: his father, Thadu, was also a director; his brother, Thu Maung, was a prominent singer and actor; and Min Lu, a reputed satirist, was another family relative of Maung Wunna.

North Marion High School is a public Double A (AA) high school in West Virginia with an enrollment of 851 students, located on US Route 250 north of Farmington, West Virginia. Although Farmington, West Virginia serves as the school's mailing address and lies approximately 4 miles from the school, the city of Mannington, West Virginia is actually closer to the school's physical location. The school is also adjacent to Rachel, West Virginia, a small unincorporated coal mining community. North Marion High School holds cultural significance beyond its educational role, as it is fictionalized as "Grantville High School" in Eric Flint's alternative history novel '1632.' In the novel, Eric Flint serves as the author and sets the story in the fictional town of Grantville, which itself is based on the real town of Mannington, West Virginia and its surrounding areas. Thus, the real-world North Marion High School, situated in West Virginia near Farmington, Mannington, and Rachel, becomes the basis for the fictional Grantville High School within the world of '1632.'

This community centers on the Ottoman dynastic lineage and the Ottoman Empire, spanning from its legendary ancestral origins to its imperial sultans. The lineage begins with Kızıl Buğa, whose son Kaya Alp fathered Suleyman Shah, according to Ottoman tradition; Kaya Alp is further identified as the great grandfather of Osman I, the founder of the Ottoman Empire. Suleyman Shah's grandson was Ertuğrul, who was in turn the grandfather of Suleyman Shah in the recorded relations, linking the pre-imperial ancestral figures to Osman I, who founded the Ottoman Empire. The imperial line continues with Mehmed II, Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, who took Gülbahar Hatun (1432–1492) as his consort. Gülbahar Hatun was the mother of Sultan Bayezid II, who himself ruled as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, and she was also the grandmother of Selim I, who likewise became Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. Thus the Ottoman Empire, founded by Osman I (great grandson of Kaya Alp), was subsequently ruled by a succession of sultans including Mehmed II, his son Bayezid II, and his grandson Selim I, with Gülbahar Hatun serving as the key maternal link connecting Mehmed II's reign to both his son and grandson's successive sultanates.

This community centers on the Argentine film industry of the classic era (Cinema of Argentina), highlighting the careers of director Alberto De Zavalia and director-screenwriter-producer Luis Saslavsky, who was born on April 21, 1903, in Rosario, Santa Fe, Argentina, and died on March 20, 1995, in Buenos Aires, aged 91; Saslavsky was recognized as one of the influential directors in the Cinema of Argentina. Together, De Zavalia and Saslavsky ran the production company SIFAL as partners. Under SIFAL, De Zavalia directed and wrote 'Escala en la ciudad,' his feature film debut, co-writing it with Carlos Aden; this film was produced by SIFAL. Separately, Luis Saslavsky directed 'Crimen a las tres' in 1935, an Argentine crime film that became his second and most famous movie; SIFAL disbanded the year after 'Escala en la ciudad' was made, which coincided with the completion of 'Crimen a las tres.' Saslavsky also wrote the film 'Allá en el Norte' in 1973, continuing his prolific career as a screenwriter well beyond the SIFAL era.

This community centers on Spanish cinema and connects a group of filmmakers and actors through several key films. **El extraño viaje**, a 1964 Spanish black drama film directed by **Fernando Fernán Gómez**, was a huge flop upon its limited release but later received significant critical recognition when it was voted the seventh best Spanish film during the **1996 Spanish cinema centenary**, an event where professionals and critics voted on the best films in Spanish cinema history. The cast of El extraño viaje included **Rafaela Aparicio** (born Rafaela Díaz Valiente, 9 April 1906 – 9 June 1996), a renowned Spanish film and theatre actress who appeared in more than 100 films, and **Jess Franco**, a famous film director who took on an acting role as the brother of the protagonist in this film. Rafaela Aparicio also acted in two films directed by **Carlos Saura**: **Anna and the Wolves**, also known as **Mama Turns 100**, and separately listed as **Mama Turns 100**, which was likewise directed by Carlos Saura. Rafaela Aparicio's life came to an end in **Madrid**, where she died of a stroke in a retirement home on 9 June 1996.

The Ballad of Josie is a 1967 Technicolor American comedy western film directed by Andrew V. McLaglen, starring Doris Day, George Kennedy, and Peter Graves; the film also featured the last acting role of actor William Talman. The Ballad of Josie was filmed in Thousand Oaks, California, with two specific filming locations within that area: North Ranch and Wildwood Regional Park, both of which are contained within Thousand Oaks, California.

Calloway County High School is a public high school located in Murray, Kentucky, formed from the consolidation of six previously separate high schools: Almo High School, Faxon High School, Hazel High School, Kirksey High School, Lynn Grove High School, and New Concord High School. Each of these six institutions—Almo, Faxon, Hazel, Kirksey, Lynn Grove, and New Concord High Schools—was individually consolidated into Calloway County High School, making them all predecessor schools that merged to create the single institution now situated in Murray, Kentucky.

This community centers on the interconnected royal lineages of Egypt and Syria in the late second century BC. Cleopatra IV of Egypt served as Queen of Egypt briefly from 116 to 115 BC, ruling jointly with her husband Ptolemy IX Lathyros during that period. Following her time in Egypt, Cleopatra IV became queen consort of Syria through her marriage to Antiochus IX Cyzicenus, King of Syria, who was her second husband. Syria itself was later ruled by the Seleucid king Antiochus X Eusebes, who reigned from 95 BC to either 92 or 88 BC. communities.report: This community centers on the House of Palatinate-Birkenfeld-Bischweiler and traces a family lineage across three generations of places and people in the 17th century. Christian I, Count Palatine of Birkenfeld-Bischweiler (1598–1654), was the patriarch of the family. His first wife was Countess Palatine Magdalene Catherine of Zweibrücken (1606–1648), also recorded as Magdalena Catherine, Countess Palatine of Zweibrücken, who was born on 26 April 1607 in Zweibrücken, the territory of which she was Countess Palatine by birth. Through her marriage to Christian I, she became Duchess and Countess Palatine of Birkenfeld. She died on 20 January 1648 in Strasbourg. Christian I and Magdalene Catherine were the parents of Countess Palatine Anna Magdalena of Birkenfeld-Bischweiler, who was born on 14 February 1640 in Strasbourg—the same city where her mother would later die. Anna Magdalena died on 12 December 1693 in Babenhausen, the place recorded as her place of death. Thus, the community links together Christian I as father to both his first wife Magdalene Catherine/Magdalena Catherine and his daughter Anna Magdalena, with Strasbourg serving as a key location connecting mother and daughter (birthplace of Anna Magdalena and deathplace of Magdalene Catherine), Zweibrücken as Magdalena Catherine's birthplace and hereditary title, Birkenfeld as the duchy and county palatine she gained through marriage, and Babenhausen as the final resting place of Anna Magdalena.

During the casting process for Ronnie Rocket, Lynch first met actor Michael J. Anderson, an encounter that would prove significant for both their careers even though the Ronnie Rocket project itself was ultimately shelved. Instead of completing Ronnie Rocket, Lynch pivoted to direct The Elephant Man, a 1980 film based on an existing script, effectively setting aside the Ronnie Rocket project in favor of this new endeavor. Despite Ronnie Rocket never being completed, the connection Lynch formed with Michael J. Anderson during its casting phase bore fruit later in their respective careers: Lynch subsequently cast Anderson in two of his later, more prominent productions—Twin Peaks and Mulholland Drive—demonstrating how the unrealized Ronnie Rocket project nonetheless served as a crucial link in an ongoing creative collaboration between director and actor across multiple decades of Lynch's filmography.

This community centers on the La Tremoille family, a French noble house, and traces a specific lineage within it. This community centers on the Egyptian noblewoman Tjuyu, whose family relationships link several key figures of ancient Egyptian royalty.
